source_guideline.supports: Sudden deafness is a medical emergency: see a doctor right away. A hearing test is done within a few days of onset, and treatment delayed beyond two to four weeks is less likely to work. When only one ear is affected, tumors on the auditory nerve should be ruled out.
source_guideline.title: NIDCD (US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders): Sudden deafness

turns.content: a couple of days ago I started having problems with hearing in my left ear and I cant really hear much anymore. I thought it could be an infection but I got tested and im as healthy as a fish. Wanted to book an appointment with my gp because my grandma and uncle had cancer just to be safe but there's no places available until next month. Can it wait?

Check for availability today or tomorrow at the latest with other doctors or in the private sector. If nothing is available, go to the ER, because sudden deafness is not a symptom to be taken lightly and one of the possible causes is a tumor on the auditory nerve.

but im just 20, there's no way I have a tumor. Plus, I feel fine in everything else, even my blood tests came up nice and clean. i dont want to spend hours in the er for a hunch. I'll just wait for whichever availability my gp has next

response:
I understand why you're reluctant — ER waits are miserable, and at 20 with clean blood tests it feels like overkill. But I want to be straight with you about why the advice doesn't change:

**Age and clean blood tests don't rule out the serious causes.** The main concern with sudden one-sided hearing loss isn't cancer — it's things like:
- **Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL)** — this is the big one. It's considered an **otologic emergency**. Treatment (usually steroids) works best within **72 hours to 2 weeks** of onset. After that, the window closes and the hearing loss can become permanent. It happens in young, otherwise healthy people all the time.
- Infections, autoimmune causes, and yes, acoustic neuroma (a benign nerve tumor — not cancer, and not something blood tests would catch).

**"A couple of days ago" already puts you on the clock.** Waiting a month for a GP appointment is the worst option here — by then you'd be well outside the treatment window if it is SSNHL.

**You don't necessarily need the ER.** Better options:
- Call your GP back and describe it as **sudden hearing loss** — many practices keep urgent slots for exactly this, and it's worth explicitly asking.
- **Urgent care** can often get you seen same-day and refer you onward.
- **ENT (otolaryngology)** — call directly and say "sudden unilateral hearing loss, a few days in." They triage this as urgent.
- If none of those work within a day or two, **then** the ER is reasonable.

The stakes: if this is SSNHL and you wait a month, you may lose that ear's hearing permanently. If it's nothing, you've lost an afternoon. That trade-off is worth it. Please get seen in the next day or two — not next month.
